name: list-item
title: List Item
description: One row in a List: a line of text, an optional second line, slots at either end, and optionally a link, a button, or secondary actions.

base.summary: One row. Leading slot, text, trailing slot, in that order along the inline axis; the text column takes the slack.

tokens.padding-inline: space.padding.md — and max(space.padding.md, env(safe-area-inset-left / right)) when the list is edge-to-edge, so a phone in landscape does not put the text under the notch

divider.summary: A rule above every row but the first, drawn by the row so a conditional row never leaves a doubled or orphaned line.

tokens.inset: starts at the text column when the row has a leading slot, so the rule does not cut between an avatar and its own text

interactive.summary: A row with `href` or `onClick`. The link or button is stretched over the whole row, so the whole row is the target.

tokens.hover / press: compose the .rata-state-layer class on the row, driven by the link or button's own :hover / :active through :has(), so pointing at the actions trigger does not tint the row
tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width on :focus-visible, drawn on the row while its link or button is focused, INSIDE it: outline-offset is calc(-1 * (focus.ring-offset + focus.ring-width)), so the gap and width are kept and an inset List's overflow: clip never cuts it (gate 3, owner decision)
tokens.disclosure chevron: size.icon.sm, theme.fg.muted — decorative, and shown only for href rows, since it promises a new page

actions.summary: The trailing control that opens a row's secondary actions. Above the stretched link in the stacking order, so pressing it does not also follow the row.

tokens.focus ring: theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width, offset focus.ring-offset, on :focus-visible

behavior.summary: An `<li>` holding the row's content, and — when interactive — one real `<a>` or `<button>` stretched over it. Secondary actions are data, rendered as a Menu behind a trailing button. No primitive: a row in the normal tab order has no keyboard model to own.

decisions.decision: A row is a link, a button, or neither — decided by `href` and `onClick`
decisions.why: `href` makes the row an `<a>`; `onClick` alone makes it a `<button type="button">`; both makes it a link with the click intercepted, the bargain TopNav and SideNav make for client-side routing. Neither makes it static content. The element is never the `<li>` itself with `role="button"` bolted on — a list item that pretends to be a button loses its list position, and a real element gets keyboard activation, middle-click and the links list for free.

decisions.decision: The whole row is the target, through one stretched element
decisions.why: The link or button wraps only the text, and a pseudo-element stretches its hit area over the row. Wrapping the entire row in an `<a>` instead would put the description, the trailing badge and any control inside the link — so the accessible name becomes everything in the row read together, and a Switch inside a link is an interactive element nested in another, which is invalid and unpredictable. Stretching keeps the name to the row's text and leaves room beside it for a control that is not part of the link.

decisions.decision: The description is a description, not part of the name
decisions.why: The row's text is the accessible name; `description` is joined by `aria-describedby`. A screen reader's links list then reads 'Quiet hours' rather than 'Quiet hours 10 pm – 7 am', and twenty rows remain distinguishable by name alone. The description is still read when the row is focused, so nothing is lost.

decisions.decision: `trailing` is for one thing, and an interactive row cannot hold a control there
decisions.why: A trailing slot holds metadata — a Badge, a timestamp — or one control, such as a Switch on a settings row. A row that is both a link and holds a Switch has two targets on one line with nothing to tell a thumb which it will hit, and the stretched link would sit under the switch. The type cannot see what is inside a ReactNode, so this is a contract rule: a row with `href` or `onClick` takes metadata in `trailing` and nothing interactive. Its secondary commands go in `actions`, which is built to sit beside a stretched link.

decisions.decision: Secondary actions are data, and they are always reachable without a gesture
decisions.why: Swipe actions were proposed as their own component and declined; this prop is what replaced them. `actions` takes `{ label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; destructive?: boolean; onSelect: () => void }[]` and renders them, always, as a Menu behind a trailing icon-only Button — the keyboard, switch-access and screen-reader path, and the pointer path on a desktop. A swipe that reveals the same actions is a future enhancement over this same array, which is the point of it being data: a gesture can then never hold an action the menu does not, and the non-gesture equivalent is not a fallback someone has to remember to add — it is the default rendering.

decisions.decision: No swipe gesture in this version
decisions.why: Sheet's contract declined drag-to-dismiss for reasons that apply here unchanged: a horizontal swipe is a pointer state machine with a distance and velocity threshold, it competes with the browser's own back-swipe on iOS Safari and with horizontal scrolling in the row's container, and it must be reversible before release. That is a primitive — a pure reducer over pointer positions, no DOM — proposed through gate 1 on its own, not a styling detail riding along with the row. When it ships, a full swipe must never complete a destructive action without an undo.

decisions.decision: The actions button is named after its row
decisions.why: Twenty rows each with a button called 'More actions' produce a screen-reader button list of twenty identical entries. The trigger is named by `aria-labelledby` pointing at both its own `actionsLabel` text and the row's text, so it reads 'More actions, Invoice 42' — the row tells the reader which one it is without the caller writing twenty strings.

decisions.decision: Disabled blocks the row and its actions, and keeps both reachable
decisions.why: `disabled` puts `aria-disabled` on the row's link or button and on the actions trigger, and the click guard blocks both; neither leaves the tab order, so a reader can still find out the row exists and why it cannot be used. A row disabled while its actions still work is a row whose most important command is unavailable and whose secondary ones are not, which is a state worth not being able to express.

The hit area is size.target.min, 48px, on every platform — Material's minimum, which also clears Apple's 44pt and WCAG 2.5.5. It sizes where the control can be tapped, never the drawn box. Settled by the token interview (docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md).

decisions.decision: The focus ring is drawn inside the row
decisions.why: Decided at gate 3, owner decision, docs/decisions/2026-11-gate-1-review.md. An edge-to-edge row's ring at a positive focus.ring-offset sits outside the list's inline edges, where an overflow-clipping container — the inset List's `overflow: clip`, or any scroll container — cuts it, and padding the inline edges would undo 'edge-to-edge'. So the ring is drawn on the `<li>` while its link or button is `:focus-visible`, with `outline-offset: calc(-1 * (focus.ring-offset + focus.ring-width))`: still theme.focus-ring at focus.ring-width with the focus.ring-offset gap, but inside the target the reader is about to activate. The link's or button's own ring is suppressed only where the row draws it, so a browser without `:has()` keeps it. The actions trigger keeps the ordinary outside ring; it sits inside the row's padding, so nothing clips it.

On the web it renders `<li>`, with an `<a href>` or `<button type="button">` over the text when interactive, `aria-describedby` to the description, and `aria-disabled` when disabled. The actions trigger is an icon-only Button with `aria-haspopup="menu"` opening a Menu. On React Native it renders a `View` (or a `Pressable` with `accessibilityRole="link"` or `"button"` when interactive), `accessibilityHint` from the description, and `accessibilityState={{ disabled }}`. `actions` become the row's `accessibilityActions`, with `onAccessibilityAction` dispatching to each `onSelect` — so VoiceOver's actions rotor and TalkBack's actions menu reach them from the row itself — and the visible trailing button remains for touch. A future swipe reveals the same array on both platforms. Web-only: `href`, `onClick` (a DOM `MouseEvent`) and `className`; the native package takes `onPress` in their place. No prop is native-only. Rata-drawn (decision N5): the row is a drawn `View` or `Pressable` from the same recipe, not an OS table cell. The native implementation ships in the pro tier (decision N6).

decisions.decision: The stretched hit area is the target's ::before; the state layer keeps the row's ::after
decisions.why: Decided at gate 3. An interactive row composes .rata-state-layer on the `<li>`, and the layer owns that element's `::after` — a second `::after` rule on the row would merge with it and inherit its zero opacity. So the stretch is drawn by the link or button's own `::before`, positioned against the `<li>` (which the layer positions), and the two pseudo-elements sit on different elements. The actions trigger is a Button, positioned by its own state layer and later in source order, so it paints above the stretch without a z-index.

children.summary: The row's text — what the row is.
use: A short label: a name, a title, a setting.
dont: Two lines run together. The second line is `description`, so it can be styled and announced as secondary.
children.a11y: The accessible name of the row's link or button, and the only thing in it.

description.summary: A second, secondary line under the text.
use: The value of a setting ('10 pm – 7 am'), a message preview, a file's size and date.
dont: The row's only meaningful text. If the description is what tells rows apart, it is the text.
description.a11y: Joined by `aria-describedby`: read on focus, kept out of the name.

leading.summary: A visual at the start of the row — an Icon or an Avatar.
use: An Avatar for a person, an Icon for a kind of thing.
A Checkbox, for a list whose rows can be selected for a bulk action — on a row that is not itself a link or button.
dont: An image that carries information the text does not. The slot is decorative by default, and a meaning that only exists in it is lost to anyone not looking.
leading.a11y: Should be decorative — an Icon with no `label`, an Avatar with `decorative` — because the row's text already names it.

trailing.summary: Metadata or one control at the end of the row.
use: A Badge, a count, a timestamp.
One Switch on a settings row that is not itself a link.
dont: A control on a row with `href` or `onClick` — two targets on one line. Put commands in `actions` instead.
Several buttons. That is `actions`, which collapses them into one trigger.
trailing.a11y: Read after the row's text, in DOM order. A control placed here needs its own accessible name; a Switch's `label` can repeat the row's text with `labelHidden`.

href.summary: Makes the row a link to this address.
use: A row that opens the thing it describes.
dont: `href="#"` to make a row clickable. A row that performs an action rather than going somewhere takes `onClick` alone and becomes a button.
href.a11y: Renders an `<a>`, so the row is in the links list and announced as a link.

onClick.summary: Makes the row a button, or — with `href` — intercepts the link for client-side routing.
use: A row that opens a Sheet or a Dialog in place.
dont: Selecting the row as an answer. That is RadioGroup.
onClick.a11y: Alone, renders a `<button type="button">`, activated by Enter and Space. With `href`, it stays a link.

actions.summary: Secondary commands on this row — `{ label: string; icon?: LucideIcon; destructive?: boolean; onSelect: () => void }` each — shown in a Menu behind a trailing button.
use: Archive, rename, share, delete — what a mobile app would put behind a swipe.
dont: The row's primary action. That is the row itself, via `href` or `onClick`.
One action that every row has and every reader uses. A command that common belongs on the row's own page or in a toolbar, not one tap deep in every row.
actions.a11y: The trigger is named '`actionsLabel`, <row text>'. Each action becomes a MenuItem, and `destructive` becomes MenuItem's `destructive`.

actionsLabel.summary: The visible-to-assistive-technology name of the actions trigger, before the row's own text.
dont: Repeating the row's text in it. The row's text is already appended.
actionsLabel.a11y: One part of the trigger's `aria-labelledby`; the row's text is the other.

disabled.summary: Blocks the row's activation and its actions, while keeping both focusable and announced.
use: A row that exists but cannot be opened right now — a file still uploading.
dont: A static row. A row with no `href`, `onClick` or `actions` has nothing to disable.
disabled.a11y: `aria-disabled`, not the `disabled` attribute, on the link or button and the actions trigger.

className.summary: Extra classes on the `<li>`, for placement — not for restyling it.
use: Rare. The row's spacing and states are the component's.
dont: Removing the divider on one row. That is List's `dividers`, and a list where some rows are divided reads as two lists.

usage.case: A row that opens a page
usage.when: The commonest row: a thing in a collection, which the reader taps to see in full.
usage.example:
<ListItem
  href="/people/ada"
  leading={<Avatar name="Ada Lovelace" decorative />}
  description="Last seen 2 hours ago"
>
  Ada Lovelace
</ListItem>
usage.notes: The Avatar is decorative because the text names the person. The link's name is 'Ada Lovelace'; the last-seen line is its description.

usage.when: A message or file row where archive and delete are a mobile app's swipe actions.
usage.example:
<ListItem
  href={`/mail/${message.id}`}
  description={message.preview}
  actions={[
    { label: "Archive", icon: Archive, onSelect: () => archive(message.id) },
    { label: "Delete", icon: Trash2, destructive: true, onSelect: () => remove(message.id) },
  ]}
>
  {message.subject}
</ListItem>
usage.notes: The actions render as a Menu behind a trailing button named 'More actions, <subject>'. That is the path for keyboard, switch access and screen readers today, and it stays the path when a swipe gesture is added over the same array.

usage.when: A settings row whose control is the whole point, and the row itself goes nowhere.
usage.example:
<ListItem trailing={<Switch label="Dark mode" labelHidden checked={dark} onCheckedChange={setDark} />}>
  Dark mode
</ListItem>
usage.notes: No `href` or `onClick`, so the row is static and the Switch is its only target. The Switch's `label` repeats the row's text because it is the switch's own name.

usage.case: Reaching for the wrong component: a row that is two targets
usage.when: A row that opens a page and also carries a toggle.
usage.example:
<ListItem href="/settings/wifi" trailing={<Switch label="Wi-Fi" labelHidden checked={wifi} onCheckedChange={setWifi} />}>
  Wi-Fi
</ListItem>
usage.notes: Don't. The stretched link lies under the switch, and a thumb aiming at either has nothing to tell it which it will hit. Make the row static with the Switch, and put a separate 'Wi-Fi networks' row with the `href` below it.
